title: Iron Rockets and the Red Glare
summary: In India, the armies of Mysore built rockets with strong iron tubes that could fly much further than anyone else's. The British copied them, and soon rockets were streaking across battlefields all over the world, even lighting up the sky over an American fort in a famous song. Meanwhile, a genius named Isaac Newton wrote down the simple law that explains how every rocket moves.

sections.heading: A Gunner's Book Full of Rockets
paragraphs: By the 1600s, rockets were no longer a Chinese secret. They had spread across Asia, the Middle East and Europe, mostly as fireworks for royal parties and as noisy, unpredictable weapons. People who made them worked from experience, not from science. A good rocket maker knew which powder mixtures burned well, how tightly to pack a tube, and how long the guiding stick should be. But nobody could explain exactly why a rocket flew, and every maker guarded his own tricks.

Then, in 1650, a thick book was printed in Amsterdam with a grand Latin title: Artis Magnae Artilleriae, pars prima, which means 'The Great Art of Artillery, Part One'. Its author was Kazimierz Siemienowicz, an artillery expert born around 1600 in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, which was then joined with the Kingdom of Poland in one large state called the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Siemienowicz had served as a senior artillery officer, and his book collected everything he knew about cannons, gunpowder and fireworks.

A big part of the book was about rockets. Siemienowicz described how to make rocket tubes, how to mix and pack the powder, and how to test them. He showed rockets launched in batteries, many at once. Most surprisingly, he drew rockets stacked on top of one another, so that when the first one burned out, the next one would light and keep pushing. That is the idea of a multi-stage rocket, the same idea that would one day carry astronauts to the Moon. He also drew rockets with triangle-shaped fins, a shape we now call a delta wing, which could keep a rocket flying straight without the usual long wooden stick.

Was he the first to think of stages? Fair credit matters here. In 1961, historians studied a manuscript written in the 1500s by Conrad Haas, an artillery officer working in Sibiu, in what is now Romania. Haas had also sketched multi-stage rockets and delta-shaped fins about a hundred years earlier. Some historians think Siemienowicz may have known of similar ideas; others think he came to them on his own. Either way, Siemienowicz's book was the one that was printed, read and copied.

And copied it was. The Great Art of Artillery was translated into French, German, Dutch and English, and for more than a century it was used as a standard handbook by artillery officers across Europe. Imagine a young officer in the 1700s, in a cold barracks room lit by a candle, turning the pages and studying the engraved pictures of rockets and fireworks. Siemienowicz's book did not launch anything into space, of course. But it showed that rockets could be studied carefully, written down, improved and taught, like any other branch of engineering.

Still, something big was missing. Siemienowicz could tell you how to build a rocket, but not why it worked. That answer would come from England, from a quiet professor at Cambridge University who never built a rocket in his life.

sections.heading: Newton Explains the Push
paragraphs: Isaac Newton was born in 1643 in the small village of Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire, England. As a boy he built model windmills, water clocks and sundials. As a young man he became a professor of mathematics at Cambridge, where he worked on light, colours, mathematics and the movement of the planets. In 1687 he published a book that changed science forever. Its Latin title is Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, which means 'Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy'. Most people just call it the Principia.

The book exists partly thanks to Newton's friend, the astronomer Edmond Halley, the same Halley after whom Halley's Comet is named. Halley encouraged Newton to write down his ideas and even paid for the printing himself. Near the start of the Principia, Newton set out three simple rules for how things move. We call them Newton's laws of motion.

The first law says that an object keeps doing what it is doing, sitting still or moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless a force pushes or pulls it. The second law says that a bigger force makes a bigger change in motion, and that heavy things are harder to speed up than light things. The third law is the one every rocket depends on. In a famous English translation from 1729, it reads: 'To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction.'

What does that mean in real life? It means forces always come in pairs. If you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard, in the opposite direction. Stand on a skateboard and throw a heavy basketball forwards: you roll backwards. Fire a cannon, and the cannon jumps back, which gunners call recoil. Blow up a balloon and let it go: the air rushes out of the neck one way and the balloon zooms off the other way.

A rocket is just a very powerful, very organised version of that balloon. Inside the rocket, fuel burns and turns into a huge amount of hot gas. The gas is squeezed out through an opening at the back at enormous speed. The rocket pushes the gas backwards, and the gas pushes the rocket forwards. That forward push is called thrust. Notice something important: the rocket is not pushing against the ground or the air behind it. It pushes against its own exhaust. That is why, as later chapters will show, rockets work even better in empty space, where there is no air to get in the way.

Newton himself was not thinking about spaceships. He was explaining falling apples, swinging pendulums, ocean tides and the paths of planets around the Sun. Yet in the same book he also showed that one single force, gravity, holds the Moon in its path around the Earth. Together, his laws of motion and his law of gravity are exactly the tools that rocket engineers still use today to plan every launch and every orbit. When NASA calculated the path of the Apollo spacecraft to the Moon in the 1960s, it was doing Newton's kind of mathematics, just with faster computers.

For more than a century after 1687, though, hardly anyone connected Newton's third law with the fireworks and war rockets that were still being made by hand. The next big leap in rocket building did not come from a university at all. It came from southern India.

sections.heading: The Iron Rockets of Mysore
paragraphs: In the 1700s, the Kingdom of Mysore was a powerful state in the south of India. Its capital was the island fortress of Srirangapatna, which British writers of the time spelled Seringapatam. Around 1761, a talented soldier named Hyder Ali took control of the kingdom. He was a military commander who had risen from fairly humble beginnings, and he was eager to use the newest weapons he could find, from European-style cannons and muskets to rockets.

Mysore was in a dangerous spot. The British East India Company, a trading company that had its own private army, was taking over more and more of India. Between 1767 and 1799, Mysore and the Company fought four wars, now called the Anglo-Mysore Wars. In these wars, Mysore's rocket troops became famous, and feared.

What made Mysore's rockets special? Most rockets of that time, in Europe and elsewhere, had tubes made of paper, cardboard or wood. These were fine for fireworks, but they could not hold much pressure. Pack them too hard, or make the powder burn too fiercely, and the tube would burst. Mysore's rocket makers instead used tubes of hammered iron. Iron is far stronger, so the powder inside could be packed more tightly and burn at a higher pressure. Higher pressure meant faster exhaust, and faster exhaust meant a stronger push and a longer flight. Historians often describe these as the first successful iron-cased rockets.

A typical Mysore rocket tube was roughly 20 centimetres long and about 6 centimetres wide, a bit like a large tin can stretched out. It was tied to a long bamboo pole that acted like the stick on a firework rocket, keeping it pointed in roughly the right direction. The whole weapon weighed a few kilograms, and the bigger ones could fly about 2 kilometres or more. Some versions reportedly carried blades on the pole, so the rocket would slash through enemy lines as it skidded along the ground.

These rockets were not very accurate. One rocket by itself might wobble off anywhere. But a battery of hundreds of rockets fired together, screaming and trailing smoke and sparks, could frighten horses, break up lines of soldiers and set supplies on fire. Hyder Ali's army already had special companies of rocket men. His son, Tipu Sultan, expanded them much further; several accounts say that by the early 1790s Tipu's rocket troops numbered about 5,000, though numbers from that time are hard to check. A military manual written for Tipu, called the Fathul Mujahidin, even set out how rocket men should be organised in each brigade.

The rockets made a strong impression at the Battle of Pollilur on 10 September 1780, during the Second Anglo-Mysore War. There, Mysore's army defeated a large British force under Colonel William Baillie. According to accounts of the battle, a rocket or shell may have set off the British ammunition carts in a massive explosion, which helped break the British lines. Historians cannot be completely sure exactly which weapon caused the blast, but British officers came away with a healthy respect for Mysore's rockets.

Tipu Sultan, who was born in 1751 and became ruler after Hyder Ali died in 1782, was clever, well educated and interested in science and new technology. He was also a tough opponent who kept fighting the British for most of his reign. His tiger symbol appeared on his flags, his weapons and even his throne, and he was nicknamed the Tiger of Mysore.

sections.heading: The Fall of the Tiger's Fortress
paragraphs: In 1792, at the end of the Third Anglo-Mysore War, a British-led army reached Seringapatam. Once again, Tipu's rocket troops fired volley after volley, especially at night, when the glowing trails made them even more alarming. Tipu lost that war and had to give up about half of his kingdom, but he kept his throne and his fortress.

Seven years later, in 1799, the British came back for the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War. A large army, including thousands of Indian soldiers serving the East India Company and troops from the neighbouring state of Hyderabad, marched on Seringapatam and surrounded it. Among the British officers was a young colonel named Arthur Wellesley, who would later become famous as the Duke of Wellington. During the siege, Mysore's rockets again harassed the attackers, especially during night fighting in the groves and trenches around the fort.

On 4 May 1799, British-led troops broke through a gap blasted in the walls and stormed the city. Tipu Sultan died fighting near one of the gates. With him ended the independent Kingdom of Mysore as a great power; the British put a young member of the old royal family on the throne, under their control.

Inside the captured fortress, the British found warehouses full of weapons. Among them, according to the usual count, were about 700 rockets ready for use, around 600 launchers and some 9,000 empty rocket cases. Some of these were packed up and shipped thousands of kilometres to England, to the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich, near London, where the British army tested and stored its weapons. A few Mysore rockets survive today in museums, a reminder that one of the key steps in rocket history happened in India.

It is worth pausing on that. When people tell the story of rockets, they sometimes jump straight from ancient China to European and American scientists. But the iron rockets of Mysore were a real engineering advance, made by Indian craftsmen and soldiers. Many Indians today are proud of this history. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, a rocket engineer who helped build India's space and missile programmes and later became President of India, often spoke of Tipu's rockets as an early chapter in his country's long story with rocketry.

sections.heading: Congreve Copies and Improves
paragraphs: At Woolwich, the captured rockets caught the eye of a young Englishman named William Congreve. Born on 20 May 1772, he was the son of another William Congreve, an army general who was in charge of the Royal Laboratory at Woolwich Arsenal. The younger Congreve had studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, the same college where Newton had once worked. He was full of ideas and inventions, and he was very good at persuading important people to support them.

Around 1804, Congreve began studying rockets seriously. He bought the best rockets he could find in London, took apart Indian examples, and ran test after test. His early rockets flew only a few hundred metres, much less than the Mysore weapons, so he experimented with stronger iron cases, better powder and different shapes. By 1805 he could show his rockets to the British Prime Minister, William Pitt the Younger, who agreed to fund more work.

Congreve's finished rockets came in a whole family of sizes, named by weight, like cannon balls. There were small ones of a few pounds, and huge ones of 100 pounds or more. The most common was the 32-pounder, about 14.5 kilograms. Its iron case was a bit over a metre long and about 10 centimetres wide, and it was attached to a long wooden guide stick around 4.5 metres long. These rockets could reach about 2.7 kilometres, roughly 9,000 feet. They could carry an explosive or fire-starting charge in the nose, or a load of small metal balls that burst over enemy troops.

The great advantage of rockets was that they needed no heavy cannon. A cannon that could throw a large shell weighed tonnes and needed a team of horses to pull it. A rocket was launched from a simple frame or tube, or even from the ground. A small boat could carry rocket launchers. That made rockets perfect for the British Royal Navy, which could carry them close to enemy coasts.

Congreve's rockets went into action against Napoleon's France. On 8 October 1806, British boats fired a barrage of about 2,000 rockets at the French port of Boulogne, where Napoleon had once gathered an army to invade England, and parts of the town caught fire. In 1807, during the British attack on Copenhagen in Denmark, cannons, mortars and rockets set large parts of the city ablaze. In October 1813, at the huge Battle of Leipzig in Germany, a small British Rocket Troop fought alongside Britain's allies; its commander, Captain Richard Bogue, was killed there.

Rockets were scary, but they were still wild. Their flight could be thrown off by a gust of wind, by uneven burning, or by the long stick catching on something. Some rockets even curved around and came back toward the people who had fired them. Many soldiers were not impressed. Others thought rockets were worth it for their shock value and the fires they could start. Congreve, for his part, kept improving his designs, writing books about his rocket system, and even proposing rockets for whaling and for firing rescue lines to shipwrecks.

sections.heading: The Rockets' Red Glare
paragraphs: Meanwhile, across the Atlantic, Britain was at war with the young United States. The War of 1812 lasted from 1812 to early 1815, and Congreve's rockets crossed the ocean with the Royal Navy. On 24 August 1814, at the Battle of Bladensburg in Maryland, British rockets screeched over the inexperienced American militia, and many of them fled. That same evening, British troops marched into Washington, D.C., and set fire to the White House and the Capitol.

Next, the British turned toward the busy port city of Baltimore. To reach it by sea, their warships had to get past Fort McHenry, a star-shaped brick fort guarding the harbour, commanded by Major George Armistead. At about 6:30 in the morning on 13 September 1814, British ships began a bombardment that went on through the day and the stormy night, about 25 hours in all.

The main weapons were bomb ships, which fired heavy exploding shells high into the air with mortars, so that they came down on the fort from above. The British fired an estimated 1,500 to 1,800 shells and rockets. A special rocket ship, HMS Erebus, launched 32-pounder Congreve rockets, whose fiery trails arced across the dark, rainy sky. The fort's own cannons could not reach most of the British ships, so the defenders mostly had to wait and endure. One American soldier later said they felt like pigeons tied by the legs to be shot at.

Watching from a ship several kilometres away was a 35-year-old American lawyer and amateur poet named Francis Scott Key. He had sailed out to the British fleet to arrange the release of a friend, Dr William Beanes, who had been taken prisoner. The British agreed to free Beanes but would not let the Americans go until the attack was over, because they had seen the British plans. So Key spent the long night on a small American truce ship, staring toward the fort, trying to see through the smoke, rain and darkness whether it had surrendered.

Every flash of a bursting shell and every streak of a rocket lit up the fort for a moment. In the morning of 14 September, as the firing stopped, the soldiers at Fort McHenry raised a huge garrison flag, about 9 by 13 metres (30 by 42 feet), sewn by the Baltimore flag maker Mary Pickersgill and her helpers. When Key saw the Stars and Stripes still flying, he knew the fort had held.

Deeply moved, Key wrote a poem about that night, first called 'Defence of Fort M'Henry'. It describes 'the rockets' red glare, the bombs bursting in air' giving 'proof through the night that our flag was still there'. The poem was soon printed and sung to the tune of a popular British song. It became known as 'The Star-Spangled Banner', and in 1931 the US Congress made it the official national anthem of the United States. The great flag itself survives and is cared for today at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington.

There is a funny twist to the story. For all their noise and glare, the rockets did very little real damage at Fort McHenry. The fort was only lightly damaged, and only four of its defenders were killed, with about two dozen wounded. The British could not get past the fort, and their attack on Baltimore failed. So one of the most famous mentions of rockets in history celebrates a night when rockets lost the battle. Still, every time Americans sing their anthem at a baseball game or the Olympics, they are singing about Congreve's rockets, copied from the iron rockets of Mysore.

sections.heading: Spinning Rockets and the Long Goodbye
paragraphs: The biggest problem with Congreve rockets was that long wooden stick. It was heavy, clumsy to carry, and not very good at keeping the rocket on course. An English inventor named William Hale, born in 1797 in Colchester, thought he could do better. He noticed something that every footballer and every rifle maker knows: a spinning object flies straighter. A rifle bullet spins because of spiral grooves inside the barrel, and the spin keeps it from tumbling.

In 1844, Hale patented a stickless rocket. Instead of a guide stick, part of the rocket's exhaust escaped through angled holes and pushed against small curved vanes near the tail. This made the rocket spin rapidly as it flew, like a spinning top racing through the air. The spin evened out small wobbles and uneven burning, so the rocket flew much more accurately. Hale's rockets were among the first spin-stabilised rockets in history, and the same basic idea of using spin to steady a rocket is still used on some rockets and spacecraft today.

The United States Army was first to use Hale rockets in battle, during the Mexican–American War. In March 1847, an American rocket brigade of around 150 men fired hundreds of Hale rockets during the siege of Veracruz, the Mexican port city, which surrendered on 29 March. The British army tried Hale rockets in the Crimean War in the 1850s and officially adopted them in 1867. Austria had its own rocket corps too, and rockets were used in a number of colonial wars in Africa and Asia.

But by then, rockets were losing a race they could not win. In the middle and late 1800s, factories in Britain, Germany, France and the United States were making far better cannons. New cannons had spiral grooves inside their barrels, called rifling, which made their shells spin, just like Hale's rockets but with far more power. They loaded from the back instead of the muzzle, which was faster and safer. They were made of strong steel and could hit targets many kilometres away with impressive accuracy. Compared with these guns, black-powder rockets were weak, short-ranged and unreliable.

One by one, armies retired their rocket troops. Hale rockets lingered in British service for decades, but they were already old-fashioned by about 1900 and were officially declared obsolete in 1919. Rockets did not disappear completely, though. They found peaceful jobs. Coastguards used rockets to fire ropes out to ships stranded on rocks, so sailors could be pulled to safety; a two-stage rescue rocket designed by Edward Boxer in the 1860s was used for many years to throw lifelines to ships. Sailors used rocket flares to call for help. Whalers tried harpoon rockets. And of course, fireworks kept lighting up festivals and celebrations, just as they had in China centuries before.

By the end of the 1800s, a person could easily have concluded that the rocket's story was almost over: an old weapon replaced by better guns, kept alive mainly for rescues and parties. Yet hidden inside every rocket was the same simple principle Newton had described in 1687. A rocket does not need air, ground or anything else to push against. It carries everything it needs inside itself. A few dreamers were about to realise that this made the humble rocket perfect for a place where there is nothing to push against at all: outer space.

deepDive: Why did iron make such a difference? A rocket's push depends on how much gas it throws out each second and how fast that gas leaves the nozzle. Black powder burns faster and makes gas faster when it is under higher pressure, but a paper or wooden tube can only take a little pressure before it splits. Hammered iron let Mysore's makers pack more powder, more densely, into a smaller tube and burn it at higher pressure. Even so, black powder is a weak propellant by modern standards: its exhaust leaves at well under one kilometre per second, compared with roughly 2.5 to 4.5 kilometres per second for modern rocket engines. That is one reason no black-powder rocket could ever have reached space. Historians also debate how much Congreve truly owed to Mysore. Congreve himself acknowledged Indian rockets as a starting point, and captured rockets were sent to Woolwich after 1799, but British rocket experiments had earlier roots too, and Congreve's real achievement was turning rockets into a standardised, mass-produced weapon system with fixed sizes, launchers and drill. Another debate concerns Siemienowicz and the older manuscript of Conrad Haas, rediscovered in 1961, which shows similar multi-stage and finned rockets. Ideas often appear independently when people work on the same problems, and the line between borrowing and parallel invention can be hard to draw from surviving documents. Newton's third law, finally, is often misunderstood. The action and the reaction act on different objects: the rocket pushes the gas, the gas pushes the rocket. They do not cancel each other out, because they are not acting on the same thing. Newton's second law then tells you how much the rocket speeds up: the same push gives a light rocket a bigger change in speed than a heavy one. This is why rocket designers are obsessed with saving weight, a theme that would dominate the next 200 years of rocketry. The decline of war rockets after the 1860s is a good example of how a technology can stall: rifled, breech-loading steel guns simply did the job better until liquid fuels and precise guidance changed the equation in the 20th century.
funFact: The famous line about 'the rockets' red glare' in the US national anthem describes a night when the rockets did very little harm: Fort McHenry survived a 25-hour bombardment with only four defenders killed.
